newsitem.title: UK: Regan's Lanica says anticipates relisting.
newsitem.headline: Regan's Lanica says anticipates relisting.

text.p: Lanica, the Guernsey based investment trust run by entrepreneur Andrew Regan, said on Friday its stock exchange listing should be restored once it has published its annual results later this month and clarified its legal position with relation to a damages claim against it by the Co-operative Wholesale Society.

Lanica, whose offshoot Galileo recently failed in a 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) attempt to take over the Co-op, said Regan and David Lyons, both shareholders and directors, would contest "vigorously" a private prosecution brought against them by CWS. Lanica's shares were suspended in February at 19.50 pounds each.

Lanica said CWS, which recently succeeded in fighting off the Galileo bid, was seeking unquantified damages against it and a number of other parties. "A statement of claim is required to be served by CWS shortly at which time Lanica will seek legal advice as to the extent of its liability," the company said in a statement.

Its shares were star performers in 1996, they staged a phenomenal rise after Regan took over when the stock was trading at 203 pence. But they were suspended on February 10 when it emerged that Galileo was considering an approach to CWS.

The bid has been one of the most controversial in recent City memory and has led to a humiliating climbdown for British merchant bank Hambros, which advised Lanica and Galileo, after it was revealed in court that a former CWS senior executive had leaked numerous confidential papers to Regan.

Regan and Lyons said the documents were offered voluntarily, but CWS obtained a court injunction prohibiting their use. It has also said it will pursue Regan, Lyons, Lanica and Galileo and the former CWS manager in the courts.

In a related development, Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) has said it is investigating the circumstances of a controversial contract agreed in January 1995 between CWS and Hobson Group, of which Regan was then the head. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
